sentences.text: The premise holds on this record without strain: two consecutive quarterly filings put Data Center growth on a year earlier at 92% and then 117%, so the segment is not only growing but growing faster.

Data Center is not one part among several but nearly the whole company, so the claim is in effect a claim about total revenue, and the bridge shows it supplied +102.5 percentage points of the +105.9% total growth.

The fiscal-year basis tells a different story from the quarterly one: annual Data Center growth slowed by 74.2 percentage points, while quarterly revenue growth has since sped up by 20.6 percentage points, so the slowdown belongs to the older annual comparison and the newest quarters point the other way.

What the claim does not carry is the step to the decision: holding overweight into the next report needs the growth to continue past the newest 10-Q, and the record's only forward-looking item is the filing's own warning that faster product transitions may make revenue volatile.

The quality of the growth carries a caution, since receivables grew faster than revenue and receivable days rose to 59.6 from 54.1, a result the corollary marks as running against what the claim implies.

An 8-K filed after the newest quarter reports the CEO's resignation effective immediately with the CFO as interim CEO, an event the revenue record cannot weigh but which bears directly on holding into the next report.
Revenue rose in each of the 8 quarters reviewed, so the latest year-over-year gain is the continuation of a run rather than a single strong comparison.
Data Center's share of revenue rose to 92.5% from 87.9%, meaning the segment outgrew the company it already dominates.
Sequential growth of 18% in the latest quarter, attributed to the Blackwell Ultra ramp, shows momentum within the year, not only against a weak base.
Concentration cuts both ways: with Data Center at 92.5% of revenue, any interruption in the segment the filing flags as volatile has almost nothing else in the business to offset it.
Receivables growing +126.8% against revenue's +105.9% means a growing part of reported sales is not yet cash, and the record has no deferred revenue to show whether orders back the next quarter.

Leadership turnover has run through the year, from the chief accounting officer and the head of worldwide field operations to the CEO himself, and the record cannot say whether it touches sales execution.
Whether the next filing shows revenue continuing its sequential rise, the only evidence that would extend the claim past the quarter ended 2026-07-26.
Whether receivable days keep climbing above 59.6, which would turn a collection lag into a question about how the growth is booked.
How the CEO's departure is reflected in the next results and any related disclosure, which this record ends before.

conditions.text: Quarterly revenue falling below the $96.22B of the quarter ended 2026-07-26 would break the 8-quarter run of sequential rises that underlies the growth claim.
Receivables rising above $63.06B while revenue stalls would deepen the collection gap the corollary already flags against the claim.
A further leadership 8-K, following the CEO's resignation, would add to the execution risk around holding into the report.
